summary: Iteration 2 re-acceptance of the /dashboard skeleton-flash fix after software-engineer's revision (loop back from my own iteration-1 finding). Read all four required upstream handoffs (my own iteration-1 finding, software-engineer's fix, verifier's iteration-2 pass, reviewer's iteration-2 pass, security-reviewer's iteration-2 pass) plus loop/learnings.md in full before starting. PRIMARY JOB: confirmed my own original HIGH finding (back/forward navigation restoring a stale server-resolved initialData with no self-heal) is genuinely fixed, empirically, on the REAL component -- not by trusting the three upstream agents' mutation tests alone. Redid a live-browser back-navigation reproduction using the same method as my iteration-1 probe (throwaway dynamic ƒ routes, real Chromium via Playwright, pnpm build && pnpm start, real next/link client-side navigation, browser Back past staleTimes.dynamic=0), but closed the one gap reviewer itself named as unresolved (reviewer-2026-09-20T150500Z.json feedback[0]: 'the useful extra experiment is NOT a third run of the same probe but a different one: a probe route that mounts the REAL DashboardBody with a stub payload') by mounting the actual unmodified DashboardBody component inside the probe route, rather than a reimplementation. No live Firebase project is configured in this sandbox (confirmed via src/lib/firebaseAdmin.ts's required env vars, unset) so true real-session auth is unreachable here -- same constraint every prior agent in this loop worked around. Swapped only DashboardBody's one useAuth import line to a throwaway, memoized, fixed-value stub context (deleted after use) -- every other line of the real component (the revalidation effect, errorUnlessAlreadyLoaded, the JSX, the actual fetch call) ran completely unmodified. Playwright intercepted only the network layer (**/api/dashboard and the incidental Navbar/WalletCard calls the real component also mounts), never the component logic. RESULT with the current (fixed) code: visiting the probe painted a server-seeded stale record; client nav to a second probe; wait 1500ms; browser Back restored the IDENTICAL stale seeded value with zero fresh server request (confirming the iteration-1 precondition still holds) and zero skeleton flash; the real background-revalidation effect then fired for real and corrected the real DOM to fresh data within the observable window; exactly one /api/dashboard call happened strictly after Back. 4/4 assertions passed. NEGATIVE CONTROL: temporarily reintroduced iteration-1's `if (initialData !== null) return;` guard into the real DashboardBody.tsx, rebuilt, reran the identical probe -- the restored frame showed the stale value and NEVER healed (timeout waiting for the fresh value), exactly reproducing the original HIGH defect. This proves the probe methodology is sound (correctly fails when the defect is present, correctly passes when the fix is present), not a false positive. Reverted the guard byte-identical (confirmed via grep), rebuilt clean, reran the fixed-code probe once more -- 4/4 pass again. CONCLUSION: I am satisfied the specific defect scenario I found in iteration 1 is genuinely closed, on the real component, via a true before/after comparison -- not an inference from a reimplementation or a DOM-only mount. I agree with reviewer's reasoning that a third repeat of the SAME probe type would have added nothing; my probe was deliberately a different, complementary experiment (real component + real browser), which is exactly the combination reviewer named as the only uncovered one. All probe artifacts (app/qaprobea/, app/qaprobeb/, src/contexts/__qaProbeAuthContext.tsx, driver scripts) deleted after use; next-env.d.ts and build-generated AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md reverted/removed; git status --short confirmed to match exactly the tree left by software-engineer/verifier/reviewer/security-reviewer before writing this handoff. SECONDARY JOB: re-validated all 5 original ACs, all PASS. AC-1 (real content, no flash) unaffected by the revision, confirmed via unchanged seed/loading-guard logic plus a full gate re-run (lint clean, typecheck clean, 82 files/751 tests). AC-2 (/dashboard dynamic, absent from prerender manifest) confirmed via my own clean rm -rf .next && pnpm build plus a node script check. AC-3 (no-cookie fallback) confirmed via my own curl against a live pnpm start instance -> 307. AC-4 (no cross-user leak) confirmed via my own freshly forged, structurally-valid, bad-signature RS256 JWT against my own live instance: GET /dashboard -> 200, initialData:null, 0 occurrences of the forged identity, correct Cache-Control; GET /api/dashboard with the same token as Bearer -> 401 UNAUTHORIZED. Third independent forged-JWT confirmation in this loop, all three agreeing. AC-5 (protected files untouched) confirmed via git diff --stat (only route.ts has a diff; requireAuth.ts/firebaseAdmin.ts/authCookie.ts zero diff) AND by reading route.ts's actual diff hunk by hunk myself -- the auth block, runtime export, structured success log, and 500 error envelope are all byte-unchanged; only the DB-read block was replaced by the buildDashboardPayload call. Acknowledged (not re-litigated) reviewer's two non-blocking warnings (7->14 query doubling with a fix on record; src/db importing from src/components, type-only/erased, fix on record) as accepted trade-offs per the task brief -- neither affects any AC. Flagged the staging hazard (4 untracked new files + unstaged layout.tsx deletion; a git commit -a would silently drop the new files and produce a non-building commit) clearly for integrator, with the exact staging commands needed. Full detail in loop/qa-report.md (iteration 2 section appended).

feedback.message: Reviewer's judgment call (reviewer-2026-09-20T150500Z.json feedback[0]) that a third live-browser probe was not warranted was reasoned correctly for what it addressed -- a repeat of the SAME A/B reimplementation probe would indeed have added little. I did not do that. I instead ran the one experiment reviewer itself flagged as the remaining uncovered combination (real component + real browser), specifically because it was my own original finding driving this loop-back and I wanted a true before/after comparison on the actual production component rather than inferring correctness through two layers of proxy evidence (a reimplementation's browser behavior, plus a DOM mutation test's isolated mechanism proof). Both pieces of evidence -- reviewer's DOM/mutation reasoning and my live-component/browser reproduction -- now agree, with a negative control on my side proving the reproduction method itself isn't circular. Recording this so the next agent facing a similar 'is another probe warranted' question has both a worked example of decomposing coverage (reviewer's approach) and a worked example of closing the one identified gap directly (mine).
feedback.action: No action needed; recorded for institutional memory.

learnings.insight: To mount a REAL production client component in a live-browser probe when the component depends on a hook (like useAuth()) that in turn depends on infrastructure unavailable in the sandbox (here: a real Firebase project -- no FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID/CLIENT_EMAIL/PRIVATE_KEY configured, confirmed via src/lib/firebaseAdmin.ts), the minimum-diff technique is: (1) create a throwaway stub module exporting the SAME function signature (useAuth() -> {user, token, loading, isAnonymous, signOut}) with a fixed, MODULE-LEVEL-CONSTANT (memoized) return value -- a fresh object literal per call gives effect dependency arrays a new reference every render and causes spurious extra effect re-fires that look like a bug but are a harness artifact (this exact trap is documented in software-engineer's iteration-2 learnings and I hit it firsthand before fixing it); (2) temporarily swap ONLY the one import line in the real component under test to point at the stub, run the probe, then revert that one line byte-identical afterward (confirm via grep). Every other line of the component -- effects, helpers, JSX -- runs completely unmodified, which is what distinguishes this from a reimplementation-based probe (the 'diverged copy' failure mode .claude/rules/testing.md warns about).
learnings.action: Reuse this technique for any future 'is the real component's behavior X in a real browser' question where the component depends on infrastructure (auth, payment SDKs, etc.) that isn't configured in the sandbox. Always memoize the stub's return value at module scope, not per-call, to avoid spurious effect re-fires.

learnings.insight: When building a probe page whose whole point is to test Next.js's client-side back/forward router cache behavior, the inter-page link MUST be a real `next/link` <Link>, not a plain <a href> tag. I initially used a plain <a> and the results were silently wrong in a way that looked plausible: `page.goBack()` still 'worked' and the record card still rendered, but the restored value was a NEW Date.now()-derived seed a few seconds later than the original, not the original stale value -- because a plain <a> triggers a full browser hard navigation (confirmed via `page.on('request')` logging showing a `GET document http://.../qaprobea` request on Back), which never populates Next's client-side segment cache at all, so there was nothing stale TO restore -- the 'self-heal' I was seeing was actually just a normal fresh SSR render, not a demonstration of the fix. Caught this by instrumenting request-level logging and comparing timestamps precisely, not by trusting that 'the page loaded and the assertions passed.'
learnings.action: For any probe testing Next.js App Router client-side cache/navigation behavior, always use next/link (or router.push) for the inter-page navigation, and verify with page.on('request') that Back does NOT produce a fresh `GET document` request before trusting any timing-sensitive assertion built on top of it.

learnings.insight: A negative control (deliberately reintroducing the known defect into the REAL file under test, rerunning the exact same probe, confirming it fails, then reverting) is cheap when you already have a working probe harness, and it converts 'the probe passed' into 'the probe passed AND would have caught the regression it's meant to catch.' Total added cost here was one rebuild/rerun cycle (~2 minutes) for a categorically stronger claim than the positive result alone.
learnings.action: Whenever a live-browser or DOM-level probe is built specifically to validate a bugfix, budget the extra rebuild cycle to run it once against the pre-fix code path (via a temporary, reverted edit) as a negative control before treating the probe's pass as conclusive.
